title: The LORD Is My Rock
sum: Psalm 18 (Psalm 17 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is the longest psalm in Book I, one of the great royal psalms, and one of the oldest poems in the Bible. Its title says David sang it when the LORD rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul, and the same song closes the story of David in 2 Samuel 22. It opens with a burst of love, "I love you, LORD, my strength" (18:1), and a string of names for God taken from a fugitive's life: cliff, fortress, rock, shield, high tower (18:2).

Then the poem tells the story. Death's ropes and floods closed over the king; he cried out; and God came down from heaven in earthquake, smoke, fire, darkness, hail and lightning, laid bare the floor of the sea, and pulled him out of the great waters (18:4–19). The king explains why: he kept God's ways, and God deals with each person in kind (18:20–30). The last part is a victory song. God trained the king's hands, gave him sure feet, and set him over nations, so he will praise God "among the nations" (18:31–50). The song ends with God's loyal love to "his anointed, to David and his line for all time" (18:50).
readings: Read as David's testimony

Taken with its title, the psalm is David's look back over his life: the years on the run from Saul, the wars with the Philistines and the nations, and the troubles inside Israel. Its images, the rock and stronghold, the doe on the heights, fit the wilderness of Judah where David hid (1 Samuel 23:14; 1 Samuel 24:2).
Read as the king's song in the temple

In the Psalter the song became part of the liturgy of the kings of Judah. Each king of David's line could sing it as his own, praising the God who kept the promise of 2 Samuel 7. After the kings were gone, Israel kept singing it as a promise about the coming son of David.
Read as the prayer of Christ

Christian readers, following Romans 15:9, have heard Christ singing the psalm: rescued from death, raised by the God who "came down", and praising God among the Gentiles. Augustine read the whole psalm in this way, as the voice of Christ and his church.

views.H: The title is taken straight from 2 Samuel 22:1, and traditional Jewish and Christian readers accept it: David wrote the song near the end of his life, looking back on his rescues. The Talmud and the Midrash on Psalms read it so, and the Gospel writers' son-of-David hopes draw on its last verse.
views.C: Most scholars agree that 2 Samuel 22 and Psalm 18 are two copies of one poem. Cross and Freedman, in a 1953 article reprinted in their 1975 book, argued from its old spelling and grammar that it is among the oldest poems in the Bible, from the 900s BC; others date it to the later kings, or think an old core was expanded for the royal liturgy. Form critics call it a royal thanksgiving psalm, with a theophany (God's coming in the storm, 18:7–15) borrowed from old hymns.
views.L: The psalm was probably sung at a royal thanksgiving after a victory. In Jewish worship 2 Samuel 22 is the reading from the Prophets on the seventh day of Passover, the day of the crossing of the sea, which 18:15 recalls, and the last verse is said near the end of the grace after meals. In the church the psalm is prayed in the daily office; its first verse, "I love you, LORD, my strength", has been a favorite opening for private prayer.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the storm scene beside the crossing of the sea and the giving of the law at Sinai. Medieval Jewish interpreters such as Radak suggest that the differences between the Psalm and Samuel go back to David himself, who revised the song. The last verse points to the Messiah, son of David.
views.X: Paul quotes 18:49 in Romans 15:9 as Christ's praise among the Gentiles, and Hebrews 2:13 may quote 18:2. The church fathers read the descent of God in the storm (18:9) as the incarnation, and the rescue from "great waters" as the resurrection. Luther and Calvin read it more as David's own experience, a pattern for every believer's trust.

deep.b: For this part the writer checked the Greek Septuagint personally, in Rahlfs's edition (online at Blue Letter Bible and sacred-texts.com), at the key verses of every psalm, including every Greek reading given in a variant (those are marked "checked"). All other witnesses are cited from published editions and studies and were not checked by the writer: the Nahal Hever scroll at 22:16 (from Flint's edition in DJD 38), the Qumran fragments, Aquila and Symmachus, Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew, the Syriac and the Targum.

The Plain of this psalm follows the site's Plain of 2 Samuel 22 wherever the Hebrew of the two copies agrees, so differences show up clearly. A full table of the differences is on the 2 Samuel 22 page. The ones that most change the sense are:

  • 18:1: the Psalm opens with "I love you, LORD, my strength"; Samuel lacks it.
  • 18:2: Samuel adds "my safe place, my rescuer; from violence you rescue me" (2 Samuel 22:3).
  • 18:4: "Death's ropes" (Psalm) or "Death's breakers" (Samuel).
  • 18:7: the base of "the mountains" (Psalm) or "the heavens" (Samuel).
  • 18:10: "he swooped" (Psalm) or "he came into view" (Samuel).
  • 18:11: the Psalm adds "his hiding place".
  • 18:12–13: the Psalm has "his clouds swept past" and "hail and fiery coals" twice; Samuel has them once.
  • 18:28: "You light my lamp" (Psalm) or "My lamp is you" (Samuel).
  • 18:32: "God is the one who wraps me in strength" (Psalm) or "God is my fortress of strength" (Samuel).
  • 18:35: the Psalm adds "your right hand holds me up" and has "your gentleness" where Samuel has "when you answer me".
  • 18:43: "the feuds of the people" (Psalm) or "my own people's feuds" (Samuel); "you made me chief" (Psalm) or "you guarded me to be chief" (Samuel).
  • 18:50: both copies say "makes great" in the written text; Samuel's spoken text reads "tower".

Most differences are the kind that arise when a text is copied by different hands over centuries: letters confused (d and r), words added for clarity, lines dropped or doubled. Some may be deliberate changes for singing. Neither copy is simply older throughout.

deep.h: The God who answers in kind
deep.b: The center of the psalm (18:20–30) is the most debated. The king says God rewarded him "as my righteousness deserved", and then states a rule: with the loyal God is loyal, with the wholehearted wholehearted, with the pure pure, "but with the twisted you twist and turn" (18:25–26). This is the Bible's teaching that people reap what they sow (Galatians 6:7), put boldly: God meets each person on the ground that person has chosen. It does not make God crooked; it means the crooked find God working against them (Proverbs 3:34). The rule is tested hard elsewhere, in Job and in laments such as Psalm 22, where a faithful man feels abandoned.

echoes: 2 Samuel 22:1–51; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Exodus 15:1–18; Exodus 19:16–19; Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:3–19; Psalm 144:1–11; Proverbs 30:5; Romans 15:9; Hebrews 2:13; Acts 2:24

settings.what: A king's song of thanks for rescue and victory
settings.by: David, as the title says; in temple use, the reigning king of David's line
settings.to: God, and the worshipers listening in the temple; at the end the nations (18:49)
settings.when: The title: "on the day the LORD rescued him from the grip of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul", late in David's reign. Scholars: a royal thanksgiving after a victory, perhaps repeated at festivals
settings.why: To thank God publicly for a rescue from death, to tell how and why God acted, and to bind the king and his line to the God who keeps his promise to David. Knowing it is a king's song explains the claims to righteousness and rule over nations: it speaks for the whole kingdom.
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, with no king on the throne, the song kept alive the promise of 18:50 and taught them to expect the son of David.
views: The title and 2 Samuel 22 present it as David's thanksgiving near the end of his life (2 Samuel 22:1).
Many scholars think it was sung in the temple by or for the reigning king, perhaps at a festival of the king's enthronement.

title: The Heavens and the Law
sum: Psalm 19 (Psalm 18 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is two songs in one. The first half (19:1–6) hears the sky preaching: day after day and night after night the heavens tell God's glory without a word, and their message reaches the ends of the earth. The sun is a bridegroom coming out of his wedding room and a warrior racing across the sky, and nothing hides from its heat.

The second half (19:7–14) turns to the law, God's spoken word to Israel. Six short lines praise it: it revives, makes wise, gladdens, gives light, lasts and is right, more to be wanted than gold and sweeter than honey (19:7–10). Then the singer looks at himself: who can see his own faults? He asks to be cleared of hidden sins and kept from proud ones, and ends with the prayer that his words and thoughts will please God, "my rock and my redeemer" (19:14).
readings: Read as one poem

The two halves are tied together: the sun's heat reaches everything (19:6), and the law's light searches the heart (19:8; 19:12). The God who rules the sky by law rules people by his law too. C. S. Lewis called it the greatest poem in the Psalter.
Read as two poems joined

Many scholars hear two pieces: an old creation hymn (19:1–6), which uses El, the general word for God, and a later poem on the law (19:7–14), which uses the LORD. Joining them made a statement: the law is part of creation's order.

views.H: Traditional readers take the title as David's: a shepherd who knew the night sky and the law. They read the psalm as one poem moving from the book of nature to the book of Scripture.
views.C: Critical scholars often divide the psalm at 19:7. The first part, with its personified sun, may adapt older Near Eastern sun hymns; the second belongs with Psalms 1 and 119, "torah psalms" from a time when Israel's law was studied and copied. Some date the joining after the exile.
views.L: The psalm is sung on Sabbaths and festivals in the morning service of the synagogue, and 19:14 closes the daily Amidah. In the church it is a psalm for Christmas (because of the bridegroom of 19:5) and for feasts of the apostles (because Paul applies 19:4 to their preaching). Haydn set 19:1 in his oratorio The Creation as "The Heavens Are Telling".
views.J: Jewish tradition loves the psalm's praise of the Torah. Jewish commentators compare the Torah to the sun of the first half: as the sun lights the world, the Torah lights the one who keeps it (compare Proverbs 6:23). The last verse is said at the end of the Amidah, and many add it to their private prayers.
views.X: Paul quotes 19:4 (from the Greek) in Romans 10:18 of the gospel going out to the whole world. Christians have read the psalm as a picture of the two ways God speaks: creation and Scripture, crowned by Christ, the Word. The church fathers saw Christ in the bridegroom and the strong runner of 19:5.

deep.h: The book of nature and the book of Scripture
deep.b: The psalm is the Bible's classic text for what theologians call "general" and "special" revelation. The sky tells everyone something about God (19:1–4), but it uses no words. The law tells Israel what God wants, and it does use words (19:7–11). The psalmist does not set one against the other. Christian thinkers have built very different theories on the passage: Thomas Aquinas held that reason can know from creation that God exists; Calvin said creation shows God's glory clearly but sinners need Scripture to read it rightly; Karl Barth denied any natural knowledge of God apart from Christ. Psalm 19 itself simply moves from the sky to the law to a humble prayer for forgiveness, as if both books lead to the same place: a person before God asking to be made clean.

echoes: Genesis 1:1–19; Romans 1:19–20; Romans 10:18; Psalm 8:1–9; Psalm 1:1–3; Psalm 119:1–176; Deuteronomy 4:6–8; Job 38:31–33; Ezekiel 3:3

settings.what: A hymn to God's glory in the sky and in his law, ending in a prayer
settings.by: David, according to the title; the voice is a single worshiper
settings.when: No occasion is given. Scholars think it was sung at morning worship, as the sun rose, or used in teaching the law
settings.why: To lead worshipers from the wordless witness of the sky to the clear words of God's law, and from praise of the law to an honest prayer for forgiveness. Knowing that the law was sung, not only read, shows how Israel felt about it: as a gift, not a burden.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, who gathered around the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8), sang it as the joy of a people shaped by Torah.
views: The traditional view: David, or one poet, wrote both halves as a single meditation.
Many critical scholars: an old creation hymn and a later Torah poem were joined, perhaps after the exile.

title: May the LORD Answer You
sum: Psalm 20 (Psalm 19 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is a prayer for the king before battle. The people pray that God will answer him in his day of trouble, send help from the holy place in Zion, accept his offerings, and give him what his heart wants (20:1–5). They promise to cheer his victory and lift their banners in God's name.

Then one voice speaks with sudden certainty: "Now I know it: the LORD has rescued his anointed" (20:6). The enemy has chariots and horses, but Israel calls on the LORD's name; the enemy has fallen, and Israel stands tall (20:7–8). The psalm ends with the cry "LORD, save!" and a prayer that the King, God himself, will answer them when they call (20:9).

views.H: Traditional readers take the title as David's and the setting as a war of his reign, such as the Ammonite war (2 Samuel 10), or any campaign of a king of Judah. Some have linked it with Jehoshaphat's prayer before battle (2 Chronicles 20).
views.C: Gunkel and Mowinckel classed Psalm 20 as a royal psalm used in a temple ceremony before war: a sacrifice by the king, a prayer by the people, an oracle by a priest or prophet (between 20:5 and 20:6), and a response. A version of 20:1–5 in Aramaic, written in Egyptian Demotic script in Papyrus Amherst 63 (about 300s BC), shows that a similar prayer was used outside Israel; scholars debate how the two are related.
views.L: Jews say Psalm 20 every weekday morning near the end of the service, and leave it out on days of joy when no plea is needed. In older Christian liturgies its last verse, in Latin, was the prayer for the king or ruler.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads it as a prayer for Israel in its "day of trouble", from the patriarch Jacob onward. Rashi explains why the psalm names "Jacob's God": Jacob was the one who said God answered him "on the day of my trouble" (Genesis 35:3), and 20:7 is often quoted against trusting in military power.
views.X: Christians read it as the church praying for Christ, the anointed king, as he goes into his great battle with death; and as a model of praying for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2). 20:7 has been one of the most quoted verses about trusting God more than weapons.

echoes: 21:1–13; 2 Chronicles 20:1–30; 1 Samuel 13:9–12; 1 Samuel 17:45–47; Deuteronomy 17:16; Deuteronomy 20:1–4; Isaiah 31:1; Proverbs 21:31; 1 Timothy 2:1–2

settings.what: The people's prayer for the king before battle
settings.by: The congregation, with one voice (a priest, a prophet or the king) in 20:6
settings.to: The king (20:1–5), then the people (20:6–8), then God (20:9)
settings.when: Before the army marched, as the king offered sacrifice at the temple, according to most scholars
settings.why: To put the king and his army in God's hands before war, and to strengthen everyone's confidence that the battle belongs to the LORD, not to chariots. Knowing it was sung before the fighting makes 20:6–8 a statement of faith about an outcome not yet seen.
settings.readers: After the monarchy, the psalm was prayed for Israel itself in its days of trouble, and as a hope for the coming anointed king.
views: Gunkel, Mowinckel and most form critics: a temple ceremony when the king went to war.
A prayer for any time of trouble
Many readers note that the psalm names no enemy and fits any crisis of king and people.

title: The King Rejoices in Your Strength
sum: Psalm 21 (Psalm 20 in the Greek and Latin numbering) answers Psalm 20. There the people prayed that God would give the king his heart's desire (20:4); here they thank God that he has (21:2). God met the king with blessings, set a gold crown on his head, gave him the long life he asked for, and clothed him with splendor and majesty (21:1–6). The king trusts the LORD, and God's loyal love keeps him from falling (21:7).

The second half looks ahead to victory. The king, or God, will track down every enemy and burn them like a furnace; their plots will fail and they will turn and run (21:8–12). The psalm ends as it began, with God's strength: "Rise up, LORD, in your strength!" (21:13).

views.H: Traditional readers take the psalm as David's, or as written for him, after a victory or at his coronation. Some link the crown of 21:3 to the crown David took at Rabbah (2 Samuel 12:30).
views.C: Scholars class it as a royal psalm, sung at a coronation, at the yearly celebration of one, or after a victory. Its pairing with Psalm 20 (prayer and answer, "your strength" opening and closing) is widely noticed, and the two may have been placed together on purpose by the collectors.
views.L: In the Book of Common Prayer it is one of the psalms for Ascension Day, sung of Christ crowned in heaven. In Jewish worship it is not among the daily psalms, though the Targum's messianic reading kept it in view.
views.J: The Targum renders "the king" as "King Messiah" (21:1; 21:7), and the Talmud (Sukkah 52a) applies 21:4 to the Messiah asking God for life. Rashi mentions the messianic reading and himself explains the psalm of David.
views.X: The church fathers read the psalm of the risen and ascended Christ: he asked for life and received it "forever" (21:4), and God crowned him with glory (Hebrews 2:9). The fierce lines of 21:8–12 were read as the final judgment.

echoes: 20:1–9; 2 Samuel 12:30; 2 Kings 11:12; Psalm 2:1–12; Psalm 61:6–7; Psalm 110:1–7; Malachi 4:1; Hebrews 2:9; Revelation 6:16–17

settings.what: Thanks for the king's victory and a blessing on his reign
settings.by: The congregation, perhaps led by a priest
settings.to: God (21:1–7, 21:13), and either the king or God (21:8–12)
settings.when: After a victory, or at a coronation or its anniversary, according to scholars
settings.why: To thank God for answering the prayer for the king, to state that the king's power comes from God's loyal love, and to look ahead to the end of the king's enemies. Knowing it is a court and temple song explains the language of crown, glory and "life forever".
settings.readers: Later readers, with no king, read it of the coming King Messiah (Targum) or of Christ.
views: Many scholars, because of the warlike second half.
Others, because of the crown (21:3) and the long life (21:4).

title: Why Have You Abandoned Me?
sum: Psalm 22 (Psalm 21 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is the deepest lament in the Psalter and the psalm the New Testament quotes most in the story of Jesus' death. It begins with a cry: "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" (22:1). The speaker prays day and night and gets no answer, though God rescued his ancestors (22:2–5). He is treated as a worm, mocked by passers-by who shake their heads and taunt him with his own faith (22:6–8). He clings to the God who has been his since birth (22:9–11).

Then come the enemies, pictured as bulls, a lion, dogs and wild oxen, and the body falling apart: poured out like water, bones out of joint, mouth dry, laid in the dust of death; they share out his clothes (22:12–18). He begs God to hurry, and in mid-sentence the prayer turns: "you have answered me" (22:21). The last ten verses are praise that keeps widening, to his brothers, to all Israel, to the poor at the feast, to the ends of the earth, to the dead, and to people not yet born, ending with "He did it!" (22:22–31).
readings: Read as one sufferer's prayer

The psalm is the prayer of a person, perhaps very ill, perhaps falsely accused, who feels abandoned by God and surrounded by enemies, and then gives thanks at the temple with a vow-meal for the poor (22:25–26). Every line uses language found in other laments. Read this way it is a gift to anyone who feels God is silent: it gives words for despair that are still addressed to "my God".
Read as Israel's prayer

Jewish tradition reads the psalm of the people of Israel, the "doe of the dawn", hunted by the nations in exile and finally vindicated before the world. The Talmud and the Midrash link it with Esther, who prayed its first verse before going in to the king (Megillah 15b). Rashi reads it as Israel in exile.
Read as the passion of Christ

The Gospels tell the crucifixion in the words of this psalm: the cry of 22:1, the head-shaking and taunts of 22:7–8, the clothes divided by lot in 22:18, and perhaps the thirst of 22:15. Hebrews 2:12 puts 22:22 in Jesus' mouth after his rescue. For Christians, the whole psalm, despair and vindication, tells of the cross and the resurrection and the gospel going to the nations.

views.H: Traditional Christian and Jewish readers took the title at its word: David wrote the psalm. Christians from the earliest centuries held that David, as a prophet (Acts 2:30), described the sufferings of the Messiah, since no event in David's life fits 22:14–18 or the worldwide praise of 22:27–31. Jewish readers placed it in David's flight from Saul or read it as a prophecy of Israel in exile.
views.C: Scholars classify Psalm 22 as an individual lament joined to a thanksgiving (22:22–26) and a hymn on God's worldwide kingship (22:27–31). Many think the last part was added or expanded after the exile, when hopes for the nations and for the dead grew (compare Isaiah 25:6–8; Daniel 12:2). Others hold it is one composition, a liturgy for a person rescued from death. The text of 22:16, 22:21 and 22:29–31 is uncertain.
views.L: In the Roman rite the psalm was recited while the altars were stripped on Maundy Thursday, and it is the responsorial psalm on Palm Sunday. In the Book of Common Prayer it is a proper psalm for Good Friday. Jewish communities do not use it in the daily prayers; some prayer books assign it to Purim, following the Talmud's link with Esther.
views.J: The Talmud (Megillah 15b) and the Midrash on Psalms tie the psalm to Esther. Rashi reads it of Israel in exile: "my God, my God" is Israel crying out. Medieval Jewish writers, responding to Christian use, defended the Masoretic "like a lion" in 22:16 and the reading of the speaker as David or Israel, as in Isaac of Troki's Chizzuk Emunah.
views.X: The New Testament quotes or alludes to the psalm at least five times in the passion (Mark 15:24; Mark 15:29; Mark 15:34; Matthew 27:43; John 19:24) and once after it (Hebrews 2:12). From Justin Martyr on, Christians argued from 22:16 that the Messiah would be crucified. Augustine taught that Christ prayed the psalm as head of his body, the church, so that its cries of weakness are ours spoken in his voice.

deep.b:
The lament (22:1–21) moves back and forth between complaint and trust, three times:

  • 22:1–2 abandoned, 22:3–5 but you are holy and saved our ancestors;
  • 22:6–8 mocked as a worm, 22:9–11 but you have been my God since birth;
  • 22:12–18 surrounded by beasts and dying, 22:19–21 but you, LORD, hurry ... you have answered me.

Then the praise (22:22–31) widens in rings: my brothers and the assembly (22:22–25), the poor at the vow-meal (22:26), all the families of the nations (22:27–28), the prosperous and the dead (22:29), and generations not yet born (22:30–31). The psalm moves from the loneliest place a person can be, abandoned by God, to the widest gathering imaginable. Few laments end with so much praise, and none with a wider circle.

Psalm 22Gospel
22:1 the cry "My God, my God"Mark 15:34; Matthew 27:46 (in Aramaic and Hebrew)
22:7 they shake their headsMark 15:29; Matthew 27:39
22:8 let the LORD rescue him, since he delights in himMatthew 27:43
22:15 tongue glued to the gumsperhaps John 19:28 ("I am thirsty")
22:16 hands and feetnot quoted; compare Luke 24:39; John 20:25
22:18 clothes divided by lotMark 15:24; Matthew 27:35; Luke 23:34; John 19:23–24 (quoted)
22:22 to my brothersHebrews 2:12 (quoted); John 20:17

The Gospels rarely say "this fulfilled the psalm" (only John 19:24). They tell the story in its words. Notice that 22:16 is never quoted in the New Testament; the Christian argument from "pierced" begins with Justin Martyr in the second century.

Jewish and Christian readers have argued over this psalm for almost two thousand years. Some points can be agreed. The psalm is first a prayer of a real sufferer, using the common language of lament; its pictures are not a coded description of anything. The Gospel writers saw Jesus' death in it because the details fit and, above all, because Jesus himself prayed its first line. Christians hold that its fit with the crucifixion and its worldwide ending point beyond any one sufferer to the Messiah. Jewish readers answer that the psalm nowhere names the Messiah, that "like a lion" is the main Hebrew text, and that the speaker may be David or Israel. Each side has reasons; neither needs the other's case to be dishonest. The variant at 22:16 shows the evidence.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the lion that roars back
deep.b: The speaker's first word for his own prayer is "roaring" (sha'agati, 22:1), a lion's sound. His enemies then come as "a lion ripping prey and roaring" (22:13), "like a lion" at his hands and feet (22:16), and "the lion's mouth" (22:21). My suggestion is that the psalm deliberately sets two roars against each other: the sufferer's roar toward God and the lion's roar against him. The prayer is the only answer he has to the lion, and in 22:21 it wins: the cry is heard. If this is right, it slightly strengthens the case that the Masoretic "like a lion" in 22:16 belongs to the poem's design, though it does not settle the reading. The repeated lion is noted by many commentators (for example Strawn); linking it with the speaker's own 'roaring' in 22:1 is my own reading.

echoes: Mark 15:24–37; Matthew 27:35–50; Luke 23:34; John 19:23–30; Hebrews 2:11–12; Hebrews 5:7; Isaiah 52:13–53:12; Psalm 69:1–36; Psalm 31:1–24; Esther 4:16; Wisdom of Solomon 2:12–20

They have pierced my hands and my feet

settings.what: A lament: the prayer of one who feels abandoned by God
settings.by: David, according to the title; the voice is a single sufferer near death
settings.when: No event is named. Scholars suggest a deadly illness, false accusation, or persecution; the title's tune name suggests use in temple worship
settings.why: To bring utter despair to God in words, to remind God of his past rescues and of the speaker's lifelong trust, and to beg for help. Knowing it is a prayer, not a report, matters: the speaker says "my God" even while accusing God of absence.
settings.readers: Israel in exile and under later oppression prayed it as the nation's cry; the first Christians read it as Jesus' prayer on the cross.
views: Traditional view: David in one of his crises, such as the flight from Saul.
Most scholars: a lament written for the use of individuals in mortal danger.
Christian reading: David spoke as a prophet of the Messiah's suffering (Acts 2:30).

settings.what: Thanksgiving at the vow-meal, opening into a hymn to God's worldwide rule
settings.to: His brothers and the assembly of worshipers (22:22–26), then all peoples, the dead and future generations (22:27–31)
settings.when: At the temple, when the rescued person kept his vow with a thanksgiving sacrifice and meal (22:25–26)
settings.why: To tell everyone what God has done, to share the meal with the poor, and to proclaim that God's rescue of one person shows that he rules the whole world. Knowing it was spoken at a meal explains why "the humble will eat until they have enough" (22:26).
settings.readers: After the exile, the widening praise expressed Israel's hope that all nations would one day worship its God; Christians heard the resurrection and the mission to the nations.
views: Some scholars: lament and thanksgiving were spoken on two occasions in the same rite.
Others think 22:27–31 was added after the exile, when hope for the nations and for the dead grew.

traditions.q: When Jesus cried "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?", was he forsaken by God the Father?
views: Not in the sense of being rejected: Jesus did not undergo reprobation as if he himself had sinned; in his love, always united to the Father, he took on our sinful state and spoke this cry in our name (Catechism 603). He prayed the whole psalm, which ends in trust.

The Son was never separated from the Father, since the Trinity cannot be divided. Following Gregory of Nazianzus, Christ spoke "in our person", taking our abandonment on himself so as to heal it (Oration 30.5).

Luther taught that Christ truly felt the full weight of God's wrath and abandonment, as the one who became sin for us, while never ceasing to be God's beloved Son; the cry is the deepest point of his suffering for sinners.

Calvin: Christ bore in his soul the dreadful torments of one condemned and forsaken, and this is what the creed means by "he descended into hell"; yet his faith held, since he still says "my God" (Institutes 2.16.10–11).

traditions.q: Can an infant have faith? ("you taught me trust at my mother's breasts", 22:9)
views: Yes. Infants are given faith by the Holy Spirit through baptism; Luther says the child is brought to baptism in the belief that it believes, and Lutheran teachers point to texts such as 22:9–10 and Luke 1:41–44.
Infants are baptized in the faith of the Church; baptism gives them the gift of faith as a virtue, which grows as they do (Catechism 1250–1253; 1266).

Children of believers belong to the covenant and are baptized; God may plant the seed of faith in them before they can understand, as Calvin argued (Institutes 4.16.17–20), but baptism does not depend on their present faith.

No faith can be assumed in an infant; baptism belongs to those who confess faith for themselves (London Confession 1689, chapter 29). Psalm 22:9 speaks of God's care from birth, not of a baby's saving faith.

title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
sum: Psalm 23 (Psalm 22 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is the best-known psalm in the world. In six verses the speaker pictures God first as his shepherd and then as his host. As shepherd, the LORD gives him all he needs: fresh grass to lie in, quiet water, renewed life, and the right paths, for the sake of his own name (23:1–3). Even in a valley of deep shadow he is not afraid, because the shepherd is with him, club and staff in hand (23:4).

Then the scene changes to a feast. God lays a table for him while his enemies look on, pours oil on his head, and fills his cup to the brim (23:5). Goodness and loyal love will chase after him all his life, and he will come back to the LORD's house for many long days (23:6).
readings: Read as a song of trust

The psalm is a 'psalm of confidence', the prayer of someone who has known danger and enemies and has found God sufficient. The change from "he" (23:1–3) to "you" (23:4–5) at the darkest point is the heart of it: in the valley the speaker stops talking about God and talks to him.
Read as Israel's exodus in small

The shepherd who leads to water and rest, provides in the wilderness, spreads a table, and brings his people to his house is the God of the exodus (Exodus 15:13; Psalm 78:19; Psalm 78:52–54). Some readers think the psalm was sung by exiles hoping to return to the temple.
Read in the church

For Christians the shepherd is Jesus, the good shepherd who lays down his life (John 10:11), and from the fourth century the psalm was sung by the newly baptized, with the waters, the oil, the table and the cup read as baptism, anointing and the Eucharist.

views.H: Traditional readers take the title as David's, the shepherd-king writing from his own experience (1 Samuel 16:11; 1 Samuel 17:34–35). Some place it in his flight from Absalom, when friends set food before him in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27–29).
views.C: Scholars call it a psalm of trust. They debate whether it is one picture (the shepherd) or two (shepherd and host), and its setting: a pilgrim at the temple, a person who escaped danger and ate a thanksgiving meal there, or the community after the exile. Many date it after the exile, but there is no firm evidence.
views.L: Jews sing it at the third Sabbath meal on Saturday afternoon and say it at funerals and memorial services. Christians read it at funerals of every tradition, often in the KJV or in the Scottish metrical version "The Lord's my shepherd, I'll not want" (1650). It is the responsorial psalm in many Catholic Masses and was sung at Easter baptisms in the early church.
views.J: Jewish readers hear Israel's forty years in the wilderness behind the psalm, when the people "lacked nothing" (Deuteronomy 2:7). Because it is sung at the Sabbath table, the "table" has also been read as the Sabbath meal and as a foretaste of the world to come.
views.X: The New Testament calls Jesus the good shepherd (John 10:11–16), the great shepherd (Hebrews 13:20), the chief shepherd (1 Peter 5:4) and the Lamb who will shepherd his people to springs of living water (Revelation 7:17). Ambrose and Cyril of Jerusalem read the table and the cup as the Eucharist.

deep.b: Few passages of any book have shaped English speech so much. The KJV's "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want", "the valley of the shadow of death", "my cup runneth over" and "for ever" are known to millions. Several of those phrases are interpretations rather than plain translations: "the shadow of death" divides the word tsalmavet in two (see 23:4), and "for ever" stands for "for length of days" (see 23:6). The Scottish Psalter of 1650 put the psalm into the metrical verse that Presbyterian churches still sing, and Isaac Watts and George Herbert wrote famous paraphrases. This site's Plain keeps closer to the Hebrew, so some familiar words are different on purpose.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a pilgrim's psalm pair
deep.b: As pointed, the Hebrew of 23:6 says "I will come back to the house of the LORD", not "I will live there". Psalm 24:3 then asks, "Who can climb the LORD's mountain?" My suggestion is that the collectors placed the two together as a pilgrim's pair: Psalm 23 ends with a worshiper promising to return to the temple, and Psalm 24 begins with the questions asked of worshipers arriving at it. Scholars have noted that Psalms 15–24 form a group framed by two entrance psalms (15 and 24); this theory adds only that 23:6, read with its Hebrew vowels, leads straight into 24:3.

echoes: Genesis 48:15; Genesis 49:24; Ezekiel 34:11–16; Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 31:10; John 10:11–16; Hebrews 13:20; 1 Peter 2:25; Revelation 7:17; Psalm 80:1

settings.what: A song of trust in God as shepherd and host
settings.by: David, according to the title; a single worshiper
settings.to: The congregation, or the speaker's own soul (23:1–3, 23:6), and God (23:4–5)
settings.when: No occasion is given. Suggestions: after rescue from enemies, at a thanksgiving meal in the temple, on pilgrimage, or among exiles longing for Zion
settings.why: To voice and teach a calm, settled trust in God in every circumstance, including danger and death. Knowing that shepherds and kings shared a title shows how bold the first line is: the speaker claims the King of the world as his personal shepherd.
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, the psalm promised that the God who led their ancestors through the wilderness would lead them home to his house.
views: Traditional view: David's own song from his life as shepherd and fugitive king.
Some scholars: a person rescued from enemies eats a sacred meal at the temple (23:5–6).
A song of the returning exiles
Others: the community after the exile, hoping for a second exodus.

traditions.q: Must a psalm sung in worship follow the words of the text closely, or may it be freely rewritten, as Psalm 23 so often is?
views: Divided. Psalm-only churches require a close version, as the Scottish Psalter of 1650 tries to give ("The Lord's my shepherd, I'll not want"), because the church must sing God's words and not a writer's own. Isaac Watts, from the same Reformed world, rewrote the psalms on purpose "in the language of the New Testament" (his Psalm 23 begins "My Shepherd will supply my need"), arguing that Christians should sing them as David would have after Christ came.

Free rewriting is welcome if it is true to the psalm and teaches the gospel. Luther turned psalms into hymns of his own wording (Psalm 46 became "A Mighty Fortress") and did not require a close translation.

The psalm appointed in the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours must be the text itself, in an approved translation, and a hymn based on a psalm does not replace it; free paraphrases may be sung at other points in the service.
The psalms are read or chanted in their own words, from the Greek or a translation of it; rhymed rewritings have no place in the services.

title: The King of Glory Comes In
sum: Psalm 24 (Psalm 23 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is a liturgy for entering the temple. It opens with a hymn: the earth and everything in it belong to the LORD, because he founded the world on the seas (24:1–2). Then come questions and answers at the temple gate. Who may climb the LORD's mountain? The one with clean hands and a pure heart, who has not given his heart to what is empty or sworn falsely; he will carry home a blessing (24:3–6).

The last part is a call and answer at the gates. Voices outside cry, "Gates, lift your heads high ... so that the King of glory can come in!" A voice inside asks, "Who is this King of glory?" The answer comes twice: the LORD, strong and a warrior, the LORD of Armies (24:7–10). Most scholars think the ark, God's throne, was being carried up into the temple.

views.H: Traditional readers connect the psalm with David's bringing of the ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:12–19), or with Solomon's bringing it into the temple (1 Kings 8:1–11). The Talmud links 24:7 with Solomon at the dedication of the temple (Shabbat 30a).
views.C: Scholars call it an entrance liturgy (24:3–6, like Psalm 15) joined to a processional hymn (24:7–10). Mowinckel connected it with an autumn festival celebrating the LORD's kingship, when the ark was carried in procession; others think of a regular festival procession. The question-and-answer form suggests two choirs or a priest and the crowd.
views.L: The Levites sang Psalm 24 in the temple on the first day of the week (Mishnah Tamid 7:4), and Jews still say it as Sunday's psalm. It is sung when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark on weekdays and festivals, and on Rosh Hashanah. Christians sing it on Advent Sunday, Palm Sunday and Ascension Day, and at the dedication of churches; Handel set 24:7–10 in Messiah as "Lift up your heads".
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 24:1 as the basis for blessings over food (Berakhot 35a), and 24:3–4 as a summary of the law. The Talmud tells how the gates of the temple would not open for the ark until Solomon prayed in David's merit (Shabbat 30a).
views.X: Christians from the second century read 24:7–10 of Christ's ascension: the King of glory, having won his battle, enters heaven. The fathers also read it of Christ breaking the gates of death and freeing the dead (compare 1 Peter 3:19; see Psalm 16:10). Paul quotes 24:1 in 1 Corinthians 10:26.

deep.b: Three Bible passages ask the same question at the gate: Psalm 15, Psalm 24:3–6 and Isaiah 33:14–16. None of them asks about family, nation, rank or ritual. All of them ask about how a person lives: clean hands (actions), a pure heart (motives), worship of the true God (not lifting up the soul to emptiness), and honest speech (no false oaths). Micah 6:6–8 and Jesus' beatitude "Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, because they will see God" (Matthew 5:8) come from the same tradition. The psalm's last answer, though, is about God: the one who truly has the right to enter is the King of glory.

echoes: Psalm 15:1–5; Isaiah 33:14–16; 2 Samuel 6:12–19; 1 Kings 8:1–11; Psalm 132:6–10; 1 Corinthians 10:26; Matthew 5:8; Psalm 47:5–9

settings.what: An entrance liturgy and a procession hymn for the ark
settings.by: David, by the title; in use, choirs, priests and worshipers in turn
settings.to: The worshipers (24:1–6), and the gates of the temple, addressed as if alive (24:7–10)
settings.when: As a procession, probably carrying the ark, climbed the temple mount at a festival
settings.why: To prepare worshipers to enter God's presence by naming the kind of life he requires, and to welcome the LORD himself as King. Knowing it is a procession explains the strange command to gates and the repeated question: it was acted out.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, without the ark, sang it weekly in the second temple as a confession that the LORD is King of the world.
views: Traditional view: written for the ark's arrival in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6).
Mowinckel and others: part of a yearly festival of the LORD's kingship.

title: Teach Me Your Paths
sum: Psalm 25 (Psalm 24 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is an alphabet psalm: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The speaker lifts his soul to God, asks not to be shamed before his enemies, and prays again and again to be taught: "let me know your ways; train me in your paths" (25:4). He asks God to remember his compassion and loyal love, but not the sins of his youth (25:6–7).

The middle of the psalm (25:8–15) describes the LORD who teaches sinners the way, leads the humble, and shares his secrets with those who fear him, and it asks forgiveness for a guilt that is "huge" (25:11). The last part (25:16–21) is a plea from someone lonely, poor and surrounded by enemies. An extra line outside the alphabet turns the prayer into one for the whole people: "God, ransom Israel from all its troubles" (25:22).

views.H: Traditional readers take the title as David's and read the psalm as a prayer of his later years, remembering "the sins I did when young" (25:7). Augustine heard in it the voice of Christ speaking for his members who are sinners.
views.C: Scholars call it an individual lament in acrostic form, mixed with wisdom teaching (25:8–10; 25:12–14). Acrostics are often thought to be later and more literary; many date this one after the exile, and take 25:22 as a line added for congregational use. It shares its pattern (missing vav, extra pe at the end) with Psalm 34.
views.L: In the Roman rite the opening verses (Ad te levavi) are the entrance chant for the first Sunday of Advent, the first day of the church year. In the Sephardic Jewish rite the psalm is said daily in the supplication prayers (tachanun) after the Amidah.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the psalm as a model of repentance: asking God to remember mercy and not sins, and for forgiveness "because of your name" (25:11).
views.X: Christians use it in Advent and Lent as a prayer of waiting and repentance. Its plea for God to teach the way has been read beside Jesus' words "I am the way" (John 14:6).

deep.b:

echoes: Psalm 34:1–22; Psalm 86:1–17; Psalm 143:8–10; Exodus 34:6–9; Job 13:26; Jeremiah 31:34; Lamentations 3:22–26; John 14:6

settings.what: An alphabet prayer for guidance, forgiveness and rescue
settings.by: David, according to the title; a single worshiper, with Israel in the last line
settings.to: God (most of the psalm), with teaching lines about God for the listeners (25:8–10, 25:12–14)
settings.when: No occasion is given. The lines about enemies and loneliness suggest personal danger; the acrostic form suggests a composed prayer for repeated use
settings.why: To give a whole, ordered prayer "from A to Z" for someone who needs both rescue and forgiveness, and to teach that God guides those who humbly ask. Knowing it is an acrostic explains why it moves from topic to topic rather than telling one story.
settings.readers: With 25:22, the people of Israel after the exile prayed it as their own plea for ransom from all their troubles.
views: Traditional view, based on the title and 25:7.
A teaching prayer after the exile
Many scholars: a written acrostic used in worship and teaching, with 25:22 added for the congregation.

title: I Walk in My Integrity
sum: Psalm 26 (Psalm 25 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is the prayer of someone who asks God to judge his case. He has walked in integrity and trusted the LORD (26:1), and he invites God to test him like metal in a fire (26:2). He keeps God's loyal love before his eyes and keeps away from liars, hypocrites and the crowd of evildoers (26:3–5).

Then he washes his hands in innocence and goes around the altar, singing thanks and telling God's wonders, because he loves the house where God's glory lives (26:6–8). He asks not to be swept away with murderers and bribe-takers (26:9–10), promises to keep walking in integrity, and ends standing on level ground, blessing the LORD among the gathered people (26:11–12).

views.H: Traditional readers take the title as David's and read the psalm as a prayer from a time of false accusation, such as Saul's pursuit. Some Jewish commentators link it to David's love for the place of the ark.
views.C: Scholars debate the setting. Some see a man accused of a crime appealing to God at the temple (compare 1 Kings 8:31–32); others a worshiper declaring his loyalty as he enters, like the entrance liturgies of Psalms 15 and 24; others a priest or Levite at the altar. The claims of innocence are claims of loyalty, not of sinlessness.
views.L: In the Roman Mass before 1970 the priest said 26:6–12 (Vulgate 25:6–12) while washing his hands at the offertory, the rite called the Lavabo. Today a verse of Psalm 51 is used instead, but the name remains. The psalm is prayed in the daily office.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 26:8, "I love the home that is your house", as an expression of love for the synagogue and house of study, and the verse is said by many on entering a synagogue in the morning.
views.X: Christians read the psalm as the voice of Christ, the truly innocent one, and of believers who walk in integrity by God's grace. Its handwashing has been contrasted with Pilate's (Matthew 27:24): one washes before God, the other to escape responsibility.

echoes: Psalm 15:1–5; Psalm 24:3–6; Psalm 1:1; Deuteronomy 21:6–7; 1 Kings 8:31–32; Jeremiah 17:10; Matthew 27:24; Job 31:1–40

settings.what: A plea for vindication and a declaration of loyalty
settings.by: David, according to the title; a worshiper who claims integrity
settings.when: At the temple, probably at the altar (26:6), either when facing an accusation or when entering to worship
settings.why: To ask God to judge and clear the speaker, to declare his loyalty to God and his separation from the wicked, and to express his love for the temple. Knowing it may be an accused man's plea explains its legal language ("judge me", "test me") and its claims of innocence.
settings.readers: For later Israel, without a court of appeal against powerful enemies, the psalm taught that God is the final judge of the faithful.
views: Some scholars: a person falsely accused seeks God's verdict at the temple.
Others: a worshiper declares the loyalty required to enter, as in Psalms 15 and 24.

title: The LORD Is My Light
sum: Psalm 27 (Psalm 26 in the Greek and Latin numbering) moves from confidence to pleading. It opens with fearless trust: the LORD is my light and my rescue, so whom should I fear? Even if an army camps around me, my heart will not be afraid (27:1–3). The speaker's one desire is to live in the LORD's house, to see how lovely the LORD is, and to be hidden in his shelter on the day of trouble; he will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy (27:4–6).

Then the tone changes to urgent prayer: hear me, do not hide your face, do not abandon me; even if my father and mother abandon me, the LORD will take me in (27:7–10). He asks to be led on level ground, away from false witnesses (27:11–12). The psalm ends with a broken sentence of hope, "If I had not trusted that I would see the LORD's goodness in the land of the living ...", and a call to wait for the LORD (27:13–14).
readings: Read as one prayer

The two halves belong together. Confidence and fear sit side by side in real faith, and the psalm moves between them, ending with a decision to wait. The shared words ("seek", "face", "house", "enemies") tie the halves together.
Read as two psalms

Many scholars think 27:1–6 (a song of trust) and 27:7–14 (a lament) were once separate and were joined. The change of tone at 27:7 is sharp, and the speaker turns from talking about God to talking to him.

views.H: Traditional readers take it as David's. The Greek title adds "before he was anointed", placing it in David's early years, when Saul's army hunted him.
views.C: Scholars debate unity: a song of trust (27:1–6) and a lament (27:7–14) joined, or one liturgy. Some suggest the setting of a person falsely accused (27:12) seeking refuge and a verdict at the temple, perhaps waiting overnight for an answer ("to look carefully" or "in the morning", 27:4).
views.L: Jews say Psalm 27 twice daily from the first of Elul through the end of Sukkot, the season of repentance and the High Holy Days. Christians sing it often, especially in Advent and Lent and in many modern songs; Taizé's "The Lord Is My Light" is one of the best known.
views.J: A midrash (Leviticus Rabbah 21:4) reads "my light" as Rosh Hashanah and "my rescue" as Yom Kippur; later writers on Jewish practice added that "his shelter" (besukkoh, 27:5) points to Sukkot. The Talmud discusses the scribes' dots over "if not" in 27:13 (Berakhot 4a).
views.X: Christians read 27:1 with John 8:12 ("I am the light of the world") and 27:4 as the soul's longing for the vision of God. The University of Oxford took the Latin of 27:1, Dominus illuminatio mea, as its motto.

echoes: Psalm 23:1–6; Psalm 63:1–8; Psalm 84:1–12; Micah 7:7–8; Isaiah 49:15; John 8:12; 1 John 1:5; Isaiah 40:31

settings.what: A song of trust and a plea for help
settings.by: David, according to the title; a single worshiper under attack
settings.to: The congregation or the speaker's own soul (27:1–6, 27:14), and God (27:7–13)
settings.when: The Greek title: "before he was anointed". Scholars: a person facing false witnesses (27:12) or enemies who seeks refuge at the temple
settings.why: To speak courage into fear, to state the speaker's one great desire, to be near God, and to beg God not to turn away. Knowing that the speaker faces lying witnesses explains the plea for "level ground" and the hope for a verdict from God.
settings.readers: Later Israel made it the psalm of the season of repentance, praying for God's light and forgiveness before the Day of Atonement.
views: Some scholars and most traditional readers: trust and lament in one movement.

title: My Rock, Do Not Be Deaf
sum: Psalm 28 (Psalm 27 in the Greek and Latin numbering) begins as a desperate prayer. If God stays silent, the speaker will be like those who go down to the pit (28:1). With hands raised toward the inner room of the temple, he asks not to be dragged away with the wicked, who talk peace and plan evil, and asks God to pay them back for what they have done (28:2–5).

Then, as in Psalm 22, the prayer turns: "Blessed is the LORD! He has heard the sound of my pleading" (28:6). The LORD is his strength and shield; he trusted and was helped, and his heart dances with joy (28:7). The psalm ends by widening to the king and the people: the LORD is a fortress for his anointed; may he save his people, shepherd them and carry them forever (28:8–9).

views.H: Traditional readers take it as David's, perhaps from Absalom's revolt, when false friends spoke peace (2 Samuel 15:7–12), with the last verses praying for the people he led.
views.C: Scholars call it an individual lament with a thanksgiving (28:6–7) and a closing prayer for king and people (28:8–9). The sudden change at 28:6 is often explained by an oracle of assurance given at the temple. The mention of "his anointed" suggests the speaker may be the king or that the psalm was used in royal worship.
views.L: The last verse became part of the Te Deum, the ancient Western hymn of praise, and is used as a versicle at Morning Prayer in the Anglican tradition. The psalm is prayed in the daily office of many churches.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the closing prayer as a prayer for Israel as God's inheritance and flock. 28:9 is among the verses gathered in the opening part of the morning service.
views.X: Christians read the prayer against the wicked (28:4) beside Jesus' command to love enemies and Paul's "never take revenge" (Romans 12:19), praying it as a cry for justice left to God. The turn at 28:6 has been read as a picture of answered prayer and of the resurrection.

echoes: Psalm 22:21–24; Psalm 26:9–10; Psalm 143:7; Jeremiah 9:8; 1 Kings 8:28–30; Isaiah 40:11; Romans 12:19; 2 Timothy 4:14

settings.what: A lament that turns into thanksgiving and a prayer for the people
settings.by: David, according to the title; perhaps a king, since 28:8 names God's anointed
settings.when: At the temple, praying toward the inner room (28:2); scholars suggest a time of illness or false accusation
settings.why: To plead not to share the fate of the wicked, to ask God to judge them, and then to thank God for hearing and pray for the whole people. Knowing the speaker may be the king explains why one person's rescue leads to a prayer for the nation.
settings.readers: For Israel without a king, the last verse was a prayer that God himself would shepherd and carry his people.
views: Others: an individual lament that was later joined to a prayer for king and people.

title: The Voice of the LORD
sum: Psalm 29 (Psalm 28 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is a hymn to the LORD in the thunderstorm. It opens in heaven: the "sons of the gods" are told to give the LORD glory and strength and to bow before him (29:1–2). Then a storm rolls in from the sea. Seven times the psalm says "the LORD's voice": over the waters, with power and majesty, breaking the cedars of Lebanon, making the mountains jump, flashing fire, shaking the wilderness, bringing the deer into labor and stripping the forests (29:3–9).

In his temple everyone says "Glory!" (29:9). The LORD sat enthroned over the Flood and sits as King forever. The thunder ends in a blessing: the LORD will give strength to his people and bless them with peace (29:10–11).
readings: Read as a nature hymn

The psalm describes a real storm moving from the Mediterranean over the mountains of Lebanon and Hermon and into the desert. Its point is that the power felt in the storm is the LORD's, and that the God of such power gives his strength to his people.
Read as an answer to Baal

Almost every image in the psalm belongs to Baal in the Canaanite poems: the thunder voice, Lebanon and Sirion, the waters, the king enthroned. Read this way, the psalm takes Baal's titles and gives them to the LORD, as Elijah did on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18).

views.H: Traditional readers take it as David's, praising God in the thunder as a shepherd who knew storms in the hills. The Greek title adds "at the going out of the tent", a note scholars connect with the last day of the Feast of Booths.
views.C: Since Ginsberg (1935) many scholars have seen Psalm 29 as one of the oldest psalms, closely modeled on Canaanite hymns to the storm god; some think it is an adapted Baal hymn, others a deliberate Israelite answer to Baal worship. Its repetitive "staircase" style ("Give to the LORD ... give to the LORD") is typical of Ugaritic poetry.
views.L: In the synagogue Psalm 29 is sung to welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening and when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark on Sabbath mornings. In Christian churches it is the responsorial psalm for the Baptism of the Lord, because of "the LORD's voice over the waters", and it is used at Epiphany and Theophany.
views.J: The Talmud says the eighteen blessings of the Amidah match the eighteen times the LORD's name appears in this psalm (Berakhot 28b). The Mishnah ends with its last verse (Uktsin 3:12). The Talmud (Zevachim 116a) reads the psalm of the giving of the law at Sinai: when the nations heard the thunder they feared a new flood, and were told that "strength" (29:11) meant the Torah given to Israel.
views.X: Christians heard in "the LORD's voice over the waters" the Father's voice at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:11). Some commentators compare the seven voices with the seven thunders of Revelation 10:3.

deep.h: Psalm 29 and the Canaanite storm god
deep.b:
The clay tablets found at Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast destroyed about 1185 BC, preserve poems about Baal, the storm god. In them Baal "gives his holy voice" and the earth shakes; he defeats Yam, "Sea"; he is enthroned as king; his palace is on the mountain of Zaphon, and Lebanon and Sirion supply its cedars. The bn ilm, "sons of El", are the gods of his pantheon. Psalm 29 uses almost all of these ideas, and its poetic style is very close to Ugaritic verse.

Three explanations are offered. (1) It is a Canaanite hymn reworked for the LORD (Ginsberg; Cross). (2) It is an Israelite poem written in its neighbors' style to claim for the LORD what Baal's worshipers claimed for him (Craigie, many others). (3) The likeness comes from a shared poetic tradition and says nothing about Baal at all. The first two are the main views today. Either way the psalm is not a Baal hymn now: there is one God, the "gods" bow before him, the waters are his to rule without a battle, and his gift is not rain for crops but strength and peace for his people.

echoes: Psalm 18:7–15; Psalm 93:1–4; Psalm 96:7–9; 1 Chronicles 16:28–29; Exodus 19:16–19; 1 Kings 18:20–39; Job 37:1–5; Mark 1:9–11; Revelation 10:3–4

settings.what: A hymn to the LORD in the storm
settings.to: The heavenly beings (29:1–2), then the worshipers in the temple (29:3–11)
settings.when: The Greek title links it with the end of a festival ("the going out of the tent"), perhaps Booths, the autumn feast when the rains were awaited
settings.why: To call heaven and earth to worship the LORD as King over the storm and the waters, and to promise his people a share in his strength and peace. Knowing that Israel's neighbors credited the storm to Baal shows how pointed the psalm is.
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, the psalm said that no power in heaven or earth rivals the LORD, who sat enthroned even over the Flood.

title: Mourning Turned to Dancing
sum: Psalm 30 (Psalm 29 in the Greek and Latin numbering) is a thanksgiving for healing. The speaker praises God for drawing him up from Sheol and the pit when he was near death, and for not letting his enemies cheer (30:1–3). He calls the faithful to join him: God's anger lasts a moment, his favor a lifetime; weeping may spend the night, but joy comes in the morning (30:4–5).

Then he tells his story. In comfortable days he thought he would never totter. When God hid his face, he panicked and prayed: what good would his death be to God? Can dust praise him? (30:6–10). And God answered: "My mourning song you changed into a dance for me" (30:11). He will give thanks forever (30:12).

views.H: Traditional readers accept the title as David's. Many place it at the site of the future temple after the plague that followed David's census (1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1), when his pride was humbled and his life spared; others at the dedication of David's palace.
views.C: Scholars call it an individual thanksgiving for healing. They think the title "a song for the dedication of the house" was added later, when the psalm was used at the dedication of the second temple (Ezra 6:16) or at Hanukkah, the rededication of 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). The personal story then became the story of Israel restored.
views.L: Jews say Psalm 30 every morning as the first of the morning psalms, and on Hanukkah as the psalm of the day. In the Catholic Easter Vigil it is sung after the reading from Isaiah 54, and many churches use it at Easter as a song of resurrection.
views.J: The rabbinic tract Soferim assigns Psalm 30 to Hanukkah. Jewish tradition reads the healing as Israel's restoration after exile, and the dancing as the joy of the temple rededicated.
views.X: Christians read it as an Easter psalm: God drew Christ up from the pit, and the night of weeping (Good Friday) gave way to the morning of joy. 30:5 is one of the most quoted verses of comfort in Christian preaching.

deep.h: One person's healing, a whole people's song
deep.b: Psalm 30 is a clear example of how the Psalter works. Its words are personal: illness, a near-death, a cry, healing. Its title is public: the dedication of "the house". Whatever the first occasion, the psalm was kept because a nation found its own story in it. When the second temple was built after the exile, or when Judas Maccabeus cleansed the temple after its desecration, Israel could sing that God had drawn it up from the pit and turned mourning into dancing. This is how a private prayer became a song for everyone, and how Jews and Christians still pray it.

echoes: Isaiah 38:9–20; 2 Kings 20:1–11; Psalm 6:1–10; Psalm 88:10–12; Ezra 6:16–22; 1 Maccabees 4:52–59; John 10:22; Jeremiah 31:13; Isaiah 61:3; Lamentations 3:22–23

settings.what: A thanksgiving for healing from a near-fatal illness
settings.by: David, according to the title; a person healed
settings.when: The title: "the dedication of the house". The content: after recovery from illness, when the healed person gave thanks at the temple
settings.why: To thank God publicly, to teach others that his anger is brief and his favor lasting, and to confess the pride that came before the illness. Knowing it was sung at a dedication shows how a personal story could stand for a whole people's restoration.
settings.readers: Jews after the exile, and later at Hanukkah, sang it for the restored and rededicated temple.
views: Traditional view: David at the site of the temple or at his palace.
Many scholars: a personal thanksgiving later used for the dedication of the second temple or for Hanukkah.
